name: Southern Pastaza Quechua
confidence_why: 5 independent first-hand sources agree (1 agree, 3 refine), none contradicts

new_statements.quote: El acento prosódico recae en la penúltima sílaba de cada palabra, aun cuando ésta termine en r o k. En los pocos casos en que no se siga esta regla se indicará la acentuación con el acento ortográfico. [p. 14] ... Con la excepción de los términos legales, el acento se marca solamente si difiere del acento normal del quechua. [p. 14, Préstamos] ... El vocativo, que es el caso que se emplea para llamar o invocar a una persona, emplea la vocal -ú acentuada en palabras que terminan en u; á acentuada seguida por w en palabras que terminan en a; í acentuada en palabras que terminan en í para indicar énfasis [p. 26]
new_statements.translation: Prosodic stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every word, even when the word ends in r or k. In the few cases in which this rule is not followed, the stress will be indicated with the orthographic accent. [p. 14] ... With the exception of legal terms, the accent is marked only if it differs from the normal Quechua accent. [p. 14, Loanwords] ... The vocative, the case used to call or invoke a person, uses a stressed vowel -ú in words ending in u; stressed á followed by w in words ending in a; stressed í in words ending in í to indicate emphasis [p. 26]
new_statements.citation: Tödter, Christa, Charlotte Zahn, William Waters y Mary Ruth Wise. 2002. Diccionario inga-castellano (quechua del Pastaza). Serie Lingüística Peruana 52. Lima: ILV. 367 pp.
new_statements.locator: p. 14 (PDF page 14), section 'Alfabeto y pronunciación', last paragraph; loanword note p. 14 'Préstamos'; vocative stress p. 26 (§1.3 Caso, 'Notas gramaticales')

En los pocos casos en que no se siga esta regla se indicará la acentuación con el acento ortográfico.' and under PRÉSTAMOS on the same page: 'Con la excepción de los términos legales, el acento se marca solamente si difiere del acento normal del quechua.' new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate stress = penultimate for every length); adds that consonant-final words still take penultimate stress, that exceptions are lexically marked (interjections, onomatopoeia, loans) and that vocatives take final stress (-ú, -áw, -í).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the penultimate syllable of every word, regardless of the final segment (explicitly including consonant-final words in r or k, where a Spanish reader might expect final stress). The few exceptions are written with an acute accent.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Los pocos casos' outside the rule are marked with an orthographic accent; in the dictionary these are interjections, onomatopoeia and a loan: aáw 'sí' (p. 73), aláw '¡ay!' (p. 75), áhahaha / ahaháy (laughter), tsatsáy '¡qué asco!' (p. 88, 239), kalún '[de galón] lata grande' (p. 115), kushúy (curse word, p. 142). Vocative forms carry final stress: Alunsú '¡Alfonso!', Apú '¡Jefe!', Yayáw '¡Papá!', Saráw '¡Sara!', turí / turiní '¡hermano (mío)!' (p. 26). Loanwords and proper names keep Spanish spelling; accent is written only when it differs from the normal Quechua (penultimate) accent (p. 14).
new_statements.identity_note: Tödter et al. 2002 describes Inga / Quechua del Pastaza as spoken along the Pastaza, Huasaga and Capahuari rivers in Peru (Loreto), noting minor lexical differences between a northern sector (ANDO, Andoas) and a southern sector (ANAT, Anatico); the stress rule is stated for the language as a whole, not for one sector. This is the Peruvian (southern) Pastaza variety matching Glottolog sout2990, not the Ecuadorian Northern Pastaza Quichua.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, penultimate (penultimate stress), non-strict' matches both primary descriptions: Landerman 1973 (PDF p.10, verified on the page image) and Tödter et al. 2002 SLP 52 p.14, each stating regular penultimate stress with a few orthographically marked exceptions; SLP 52 p.26 identifies one systematic exception class (vocative final stress), consistent with in the dominant set/not in the strict set. Both are SIL dictionaries with orthography notes rather than phonological analyses, and no phonology article, thesis or instrumental study of Southern Pastaza Quechua was found (Glottolog has a single descriptive ref, now obtained; the 'Pastaza Quichua' prosody literature by Nuckolls is Northern Pastaza Kichwa, a different languoid), so the record rests on the best that exists: status adequate rather than well-sourced.
